parole.significato: temperament, constituent pattern.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek κρᾶσις (krâsis, “mixing, tempering”), often via Latin -crāsia and, additionally, Old French -crasie.

parole.significato: Forming nouns relating to the jaws or mouthparts.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek γνάθος (gnáthos, “jaw”), frequently after formations in New Latin -gnatha, -gnathi, or French -gnathe.

parole.significato: Having a specified number or kind of leaves.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”) and Latin Latin -ōsus.

parole.significato: A cystic tumor that is hereditary and occurs on the chest and face among other regions.
parole.testo: From acanth- + -oma (“tumor consisting of a specified cell”) + from Ancient Greek ἀδενοειδής (adenoeidḗs, “glandular”), from ἀδήν (adḗn, “gland”) + Latin cystis (“cyst”).

parole.significato: A skin sign often associated with insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes exhibiting velvety, thickened, and darkened sk…
parole.testo: Via Latin ultimately from Ancient Greek ἄκανθος (ákanthos, “thorny flower”) + -ωσις (-ōsis, “state, abnormal condition, or action”) + Latin nigricans (“blackish”).

parole.significato: That develops, matures or opens from the base towards the apex in sequence.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄκρον (ákron, “the top”) + Latin petō, petere (“fall, rush out”) + -al.

parole.significato: A tree, Vitex agnus-castus, formerly believed to preserve chastity.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄγνος (ágnos), confused with ἁγνός (hagnós, “chaste”) + by reinforcement Latin castus (“chaste”).

parole.significato: the flexible part of the dorsal body wall behind the rigid scutum in a hard tick, particularly a female — the alloscutu…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other”) and from Latin scūtum (“shield”).

parole.significato: An eating disorder characterized by self-starvation due to an irrational fear of gaining weight.
parole.testo: From the scientific term anorexia nervosa (1957), from the symptom anorexia (“loss of appetite”), from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ν- (ăn-, “without”) + ὄρεξις (órexis, “appetite, desire”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, “-ia”), and Latin nervōsa (“nervous”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Arche, the Muse of beginnings in Greek mythology.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀρχαῖος (arkhaîos, “ancient”) (likely via Latin archaeus) + -an.

parole.significato: one of two broad subdivisions of ecology, which studies the individual organism or species.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek via Latin auto- (“on itself”) + ecology.

parole.significato: The gift of the Holy Spirit.
parole.testo: Derived from English translations of the New Testament, namely the Gospels of Matthew (3:11) and of Luke (3:16); from Ancient Greek through Latin; presumably from Aramaic.

parole.significato: book
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek βιβλίον (biblíon, “paper, document, tablet, small book”) or its descendant Latin Biblia (“the Bible”).

parole.significato: The mixing or disturbance of soil by living organisms, as opposed to disturbance of other media such as sediment or lea…
parole.testo: From bio- + Ancient Greek πέδον (pédon, “soil”) + Latin turbātiō (“disturbance; confusion”).

parole.significato: The fear of beautiful women.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek καλλι- (kalli-, “beautiful”) + Ancient Greek γυνή (gunḗ, “female”) + New Latin -phobia, from Latin, from Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: Of a galley such as a trireme: with the upper tier of rowers shielded rather than exposed.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Ancient Greek κατάφρακτος (katáphraktos, “covered, enclosed, shut up; completely suited in armour”), from καταφράσσειν (kataphrássein, “to suit in armour”) (see further at etymology 1) + -τος (-tos, “suffix forming adjectives”). The noun is derived from Latin cataphract

parole.significato: An Ancient Greek sling used to fling darts.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek κεστροσφενδόνη (kestrosphendónē) via Latin cestrosphendone.

parole.significato: Any member of the subfamily Chenopodioideae (the main part of the sometime family Chenopodiaceae); a goosefoot.
parole.testo: From the genus name Chenopodium, coined as a compound of Ancient Greek χηνο- (khēno-, “goose”) + ποδ- (pod-, “foot”) + Latin -ium. The literal translation, “goosefoot”, refers to the shape of the leaves.

parole.significato: A commander of a thousand troops in Hellenistic Greece.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek χιλίαρχος (khilíarkhos) via Latin chiliarchus.

parole.significato: The fear of timepieces.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek χρόνος (khrónos, “time”) and, in the rarer form without the n (chronometrophobia), μέτρον (métron, “measure”) (compare English chronometer (“device for measuring time”)), whereas in this form claimed in phobia lists to be from Latin -mentum (“means of, instrument, medium”), which,

parole.significato: The fear of staircases or of falling down stairs.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek κλῖμαξ (klîmax, “ladder, staircase”) + New Latin -phobia, from Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: The science or study of mathematical, linguistic, and other coding patterns and histories.
parole.testo: From crypto- + -logy, from Ancient Greek κρυπτός (kruptós, “hidden”) + λόγος (lógos, “word”); originally after Latin cryptologia, which is apparently first recorded in an English context.

parole.significato: the deltoid muscle.
parole.testo: Like deltoid, ultimately from Ancient Greek δέλτα (délta), the triangular fourth letter of the Greek alphabet, and the suffix -(ο)ειδής (-(o)eidḗs, “-like”), the source of English -oid. This suffix has usually been adapted in Neo-Latin as -oīdēs or -oīdeus (giving Latin deltoīdēs or deltoīdeus), but

parole.significato: A kind of military commander in the late Roman and Byzantine Empires, usually commanding roughly a battalion on land or…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek δρουγγάριος (droungários), from Late Latin drungārius, from drungus (“a troop”).

parole.significato: A learning disability characterized by significantly below average mathematical ability.
parole.testo: From dys- (from Ancient Greek δυσ- (dus-, “bad”)) + calculate (from Latin calculare).

parole.significato: A plant organ that secretes oil.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek έλαιο (élaio, “oil”) + -phore, from New Latin -phorus, from Ancient Greek -φόρος (-phóros, “bearing”), a derivative of φέρω (phérō, “to bear, to carry”).

parole.significato: Morbid or excessive secretion of sweat; hyperhidrosis.
parole.testo: From ep- (“upon, on”) + hidrosis (“sweating”), from Ancient Greek ἐπί (epí, “upon, on”) and New Latin hidrōsis, from Ancient Greek ἱδρώς (hidrṓs, “sweat”) + -sis; also synchronically held to end in the suffix -osis.

parole.significato: A purple semifluid substance said to be obtained from orchil.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek ἐρυθρός (eruthrós, “red”) + Latin oleum (“oil”).

parole.significato: Any retrovirus of the genus Gammaretrovirus.
parole.testo: From gamma + retrovirus. From Ancient Greek γάμμα/γ/Γ (gámma/g/G) + Latin retro+virus.

parole.significato: genetics - e.g. genotype
parole.testo: From the stem of Ancient Greek γένος (génos, “race, kind”), also Ancient Greek γεννάω (gennáō, “to produce”) and from Latin gēns (“tribe, clan”).

parole.significato: The shedding of tears containing blood
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αἱμο- (haimo-) (from αἷμα (haîma, “blood”)) + Latin lacrima (“tear”).

parole.significato: The iron-containing substance in red blood cells that transports oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body; it cons…
parole.testo: Originally hematinoglobulin, from hematin (from Ancient Greek αἷμα (haîma, “blood”) + -in) + -o- + globulin (from Latin globus (“ball, sphere”) + -in).

parole.significato: mouth blisters; a painful mouth infection caused by coxsackieviruses
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἕρπης (hérpēs, “creeping”) + Latin angina (“quinsy”).

parole.significato: Either of a pair of homonyms that have different roots
parole.testo: From hetero- + radical; ultimately from Ancient Greek ἕτερος (héteros, “different”) and Latin radix (“root”).

parole.significato: The fear of fog.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὁμίχλη (homíkhlē, “mist, fog”) + New Latin -phobia, from Latin, from Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: A small group of monks.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek κέλλιον (kéllion), ultimately from Latin cella.

parole.significato: A special type of cilium on the apex of hair cells, located in the sensory epithelium of the vertebrate inner ear and i…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek κινέω (kinéō, “to move, put in motion”) + Latin cilium (“eyelid”)

parole.significato: Of or relating to speech, words, or learning.
parole.testo: From lectic + -al, from Ancient Greek λέξις (léxis, “saying, speech; phrase, word”) + Latin -ālis (suffix forming adjectives from nouns or numerals).

parole.significato: Having an affinity for the dispersion medium and thus not easily precipitated.
parole.testo: US, c. 1908; compare earlier lyophilize (1894). lyo- (“solvent, dispersion”) + -philic (“having affinity for”), from Ancient Greek λύω (lúō, “to loosen, to dissolve”) + φίλος (phílos, “beloved”) + Latin -icus.

parole.significato: Having no affinity for the dispersion medium and thus easily precipitated.
parole.testo: From lyo- (“solvent, dispersion”) + -phobic (“having aversion to”), from Ancient Greek λύω (lúō, “to loosen, to dissolve”) + φόβος (phóbos, “fear”) + Latin -icus.

parole.significato: Excessive sweating in the armpits; axillary hyperhidrosis.
parole.testo: From maschal- (“axilla”) + (hy)per- (“over, excessive”) + (h)idrosis (“sweating”), from Ancient Greek μασχάλη (maskhálē, “armpit, axilla”), Ancient Greek ὑπέρ (hupér, “over, excessive”), and New Latin hidrōsis, from Ancient Greek ἱδρώς (hidrṓs, “sweat”) + -sis; also synchronically held to end in the

parole.significato: A giant virus infecting amoebae causing them to shrivel and harden.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Μέδουσα (Médousa, “Medusa”) + -virus. From Latin virus (“virus”). From being a virus which can turn amoeba into stone-like cysts. From Medusa, the Greek mythological figure which could petrify people with a glance.

parole.significato: Communication or discussion, especially involving academic analysis, about communication itself.
parole.testo: From meta- + communication; from Ancient Greek μετά (metá, “after, beyond; with; adjacent; self”) + Latin commūnicātiō (“imparting, communicating”); from commūnicō (“share, impart, inform”).

parole.significato: Money or currency (modern).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek νόμισμα (nómisma), from νομίζω (nomízō, “to use customarily”) + -μα (-ma, “nominal suffix”), from νόμος (nómos, “custom”) + -ίζω (-ízō, denominative verb suffix), from νέμω (némō, “to distribute”) + -ος (-os). Related to French numismatique, Latin numismat- + -ique, varia

parole.significato: A decreased production in the volume of urine.
parole.testo: From olig- + -uria, from Ancient Greek ὀλίγοι (olígoi, “few”) + Latin -ūria, from Ancient Greek -ουρία (-ouría), from οὖρον (oûron, “urine”).

parole.significato: The study of pronunciation.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὀρθοέπεια (orthoépeia), possibly via Latin orthoepia, from Ancient Greek ὀρθός (orthós, “correct”) + ἔπος (épos, “word”) + -ία (-ía, “-y”).

parole.significato: Bleeding from the gums.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek οὖλον (oûlon) + Latin -rrhagia

parole.significato: The opening of a defensive gland present in some arthropods, which secretes a foul-smelling substance to discourage pre…
parole.testo: Ancient Greek ὄζω (ózō, “to smell”) + Latin pore

parole.significato: A loud, wild, tumultuous protest, disorder, or chaotic situation, usually of a crowd, often violent.
parole.testo: Coined by John Milton in Paradise Lost as Pandæmonium, from Ancient Greek πᾶν (pân, “all”) (equivalent to pan-) + Late Latin daemonium (“evil spirit, demon”), from Ancient Greek δαιμόνιον (daimónion, “deity”).

parole.significato: Complete and universal knowledge, or a system of such universal knowledge.
parole.testo: Originally from Ancient Greek pan- (“all”) + -sophy (“wisdom, knowledge”), then from Latin pansophia to English.

parole.significato: A xanthanolide found in Parthenice mollis.
parole.testo: From Parthenice mollis + -in, from Ancient Greek παρθένος (parthénos, “maiden”) + -ική (-ikḗ) + Latin mollis (“soft, tender, flexible”).

parole.significato: A variety of toadflax having five spurs instead of one.
parole.testo: From New Latin peloria (“mutant, especially mutant toadflax”), from Ancient Greek πέλωρ (pélōr, “monster”) + -ία (-ía, “-ia, -y: forming abstract nouns”) and Latin -ia (“-ia: forming neuter plurals”).

parole.significato: Synonym of quinquennial: occurring every five years.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πέντε (pénte, “five”) + Latin annus (“year”) + -ial.

parole.significato: Synonym of quintuple in its various senses.
parole.testo: From penta- (“five”) + -ple, from Ancient Greek πέντε (pénte, “five”) and Latin plus (“in sum”).

parole.significato: A place on the other side, usually a territory across the sea from a city or an island, generally a dependency of an an…
parole.testo: Derived from Ancient Greek περαία (peraía), Greek Περαία (Peraía), Latin Peraea, often capitalized and treated like a proper name (compare e.g. the City).

parole.significato: A branch of obstetrics focusing on the medical and surgical management of high-risk pregnancies.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek περί (perí, “around or about”) + Latin natus + -ology.

parole.significato: A philosophical statement, theorem or axiom.
parole.testo: Borrowed from the Ancient Greek φιλοσόφημα (philosóphēma, “syllogism”) via Latin philosophema (“syllogism”). The Greek was formed from φιλοσοφέω (philosophéō, “to philosophize or pursue knowledge”) and the nominalizing suffix -μα (-ma).

parole.significato: One should attend to one's own flaws or defects before presuming to advise others about theirs.
parole.testo: Calque of Ancient Greek ἰατρέ, θεράπευσον σεαυτόν (iatré, therápeuson seautón) and Latin medice, cūrā tē ipsum, from Luke 4:23.

parole.significato: The abnormal and irrational fear of stickers, sticky labels and (sometimes, also) adhesive materials such as glue.
parole.testo: Coined by hypnotherapist Peter Field in 2009. Field gives the word's formation as Ancient Greek πιττάκιον (pittákion, “*sticker”) + -o- + -phobia (used to form nouns meaning the fear of a specific thing), as a neoclassical compound. In reality, this Ancient Greek word does not mean sticker, but Lati

parole.significato: Inability of the proprioceptive system to accurately interpret actual limb position or movement due to physiological ag…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πρέσβυς (présbus, “old”) and Latin proprius (“own”).

parole.significato: A peptide gonadotrophic hormone secreted by the pituitary gland; it stimulates growth of the mammary glands and lactati…
parole.testo: From pro- (from Ancient Greek πρό (pró, “before”)) + lact- (variation of lacto-, from Latin lac (“milk”)) + -in (modification of -ine).

parole.significato: Divine providence, foreknowledge, foresight.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek πρόνοιᾰ (prónoiă, “foreknowledge, foresight; providence; form of land grant”), from πρόνοος (prónoos, “careful, prudent”) + -ῐᾰ (-ĭă, suffix forming nouns). πρόνοος is derived from προ- (pro-, prefix indicating a coming forth) + νόος (nóos, “the mind; act of the mind”). T

parole.significato: A narrative technique used by a narrator to represent a character's consciousness or inner thoughts, often characterize…
parole.testo: From psycho- (“mind”) + narration, from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “mind, soul”) and Latin narrātiō (“narrative, narration”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the psychonarration technique, where the narrator describes a character's internal mental states, such as…
parole.testo: From psycho- (“mind”) + narrative (“story”), from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “mind, soul”) and Latin narrātīvus (“narrative”).

parole.significato: A metal device that sits against the prostate and perineum, through which cold water is run, used to treat impotence an…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”) From New Latin -phorus, from Ancient Greek -φόρος (-phóros, “bearing”), a derivative of φέρω (phérō, “to bear, to carry”).

parole.significato: The act of turning into a pumpkin; usually in jocular opposition to deification.
parole.testo: From pumpkin + -ification: a calque of the Ancient Greek ἀποκολοκύντωσις (apokolokúntōsis) via the Latin apocolocyntosis. From the title of the work Apocolocyntosis (divi) Claudii, a satire on the deification of Claudius.

parole.significato: A mixture of volatile hydrocarbons intermediate between gasolene and cymogene, formerly used as a refrigerant.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek ῥῖγος (rhîgos, “cold”) + Latin oleum (“oil”).

parole.significato: A form of mead made with rosehips, rose petals, or rose attar.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ῥόδον (rhódon, “rose”) + Latin mel (“honey”).

parole.significato: Any organism that feeds on detritus
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek σαπρός (saprós, “putrid”) and Latin vorō (“to devour”).

parole.significato: Any of several mixed sodium and calcium aluminosilicates which also contain chloride, carbonate and sulfate and are fou…
parole.testo: Ancient Greek a staff, or Latin scapus a stem, stalk + -lite.

parole.significato: Any beetle of the family Scarabaeidae (which includes stag- and dung-beetles).
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek κάραβος (kárabos, “horned beetle”), via Latin scarabaeus.

parole.significato: A peltidium.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek σχίζω (skhízō, “split”) + Latin pelta (“shield”)

parole.significato: The supraesophageal glanglia or brain of many invertebrates.
parole.testo: From syn-, from Ancient Greek συν- (sun-, “together”) + Latin cerebrum (“brain”).

parole.significato: A medicine that destroys tapeworms.
parole.testo: From Latin taenia (“band, ribbon”), from Ancient Greek ταινία (tainía), + -cide (“killer”), from Latin -cīda.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the lowest degree of glory.
parole.testo: Uncertain. * Coined by Joseph Smith as a nonsensical blend of terrestrial + celestial, which are the names of the other two degrees of glory. * Possibly related to Ancient Greek τῆλε (têle, “at a distance, far away”), Ancient Greek τέλος (télos, “end, purpose”) * Also possibly Latin tellus (“ground

parole.significato: The final stage of mitosis or meiosis during which the daughter chromosomes move towards opposite ends of the nuclear s…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τέλος (télos, “completion”) + New Latin phasis, from Ancient Greek φάσις (phásis, “an appearance”), from φάω (pháō, “to shine”).

parole.significato: An artificial alkaloid resembling thalline, used as an antipyretic.
parole.testo: Ancient Greek [Term?] for "heat" + Latin fugere to flee.

parole.significato: Poisoning by cheese or other dairy products
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting New Latin combining forms: tyro- + tox- + -ism; ultimately from Ancient Greek τυρός (turós, “cheese”) + Latin toxicum (“poison”).

parole.significato: Any of several cutaneous conditions involving redness and scarring, including atrophoderma vermiculatum and keratosis p…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek οὐλή (oulḗ) + New Latin erythēma

parole.significato: Digamma (Ϝ/ϝ).
parole.testo: From the transliteration of Ancient Greek *ϝαῦ (*waû) (reconstructed from Latin vau (/⁠wau̯⁠/)), from Phoenician 𐤅 (w /⁠wāw⁠/). Doublet of vav and waw.

parole.significato: A rare genetic disorder in which DNA damaged by ultraviolet light is not repaired and the skin becomes sensitive to suc…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ξηρός (xērós, “dry”) δέρμα (dérma, “skin”) and Latin pigmentōsus (“pigmented, stained”).

parole.significato: Prime matter, consisting of body and soul.
parole.testo: Most likely a blend of Ancient Greek ὕλη (húlē, “matter”) + Latin aster (“star”)
